Then they would inform people of what they had learned and claim that they know the unseen. Indeed, events would come as they had reported, so they would deceive people, cheat them, and mislead them. For this reason the Truth, glorified be He, wished to expose the jinn in this matter, and said:

﴿So when We decreed for him death...﴾ [Saba: 14], meaning: for Solomon. The word (qadaynā, "We decreed") means that death is a decree from which there is no escape, and it does not result from a cause such as illness or old age or otherwise. As we have said: death without causes is itself the cause; that is, he died because he was mortal.

For this reason the Truth, glorified be He, addresses the living, including our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), with His words: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die﴾ [al-Zumar: 30], and He addressed him (ﷺ) first before addressing his community with this truth.

The meaning of (mayyit, "dying/one who will die") is: one who is returning to death. So we, while alive, are mayyitūn, that is, we will die. As for one who has already died, he is called (mayt, "dead") with a silent yāʾ, as the poet said:

* "And the dead is only one who is carried to the grave."

For this reason, when the scholars gave us a sensory image of death, they said: "With the life that began, the arrow of death has been launched toward you; your lifespan is measured by its reaching you." So we, although alive, are dying.

As for His saying, exalted be He: ﴿It was not but the creature of the earth eating away his staff that indicated to them his death...﴾ [Saba: 14], meaning: it indicated to the jinn. The pronoun of the absent plural in (dallahum, "indicated to them") refers to what is known from the earlier context in: ﴿And among the jinn were those who worked before him by the permission of his Lord...﴾ [Saba: 12].

They said, regarding the story of our master Solomon, peace be upon him, that he worshipped God and thanked Him to the extent of the blessings and the kingship He had given him. Despite all these blessings, he would spend a week or a month eating nothing but (khushkār), which is (ridda) that we know, the last grade of flour, which we call in the farmers' language (sin), the food of the poor and slaves; while masters and the wealthy eat fine flour or (numra wāḥid, "grade one").

Glory be to God! Modern science has shown that the benefit of this (sin) that the poor eat is such that it has come to be described as a medicine, and they now make it in the form of tablets as a treatment for some diseases. Indeed, the people of luxury who lived on fine flour and fed themselves all their lives on tourist bread and qaṭāʾif (a sweet pastry), etc., come in the latter part of their lives, and the doctor forbids them all these kinds, and they find no remedy except in the (sin) and in the (ridda) which they never tasted their whole lives, as if it were an equation that must be balanced between the rich and the poor.

These researches that revealed to us the importance of (ridda) draw our attention and make us understand the meaning of the saying of God, exalted be He, and His oath: ﴿And the grain having husk and fragrant plants﴾ [al-Rahman: 12].

Likewise, our master Solomon used to worship God standing, not in a comfortable posture, so he would burden himself in gratitude to God, and would stand worshipping God until he became tired, then he would shift his weight between his feet, and then he would lean on a staff from the intensity of his fatigue.

God decreed death upon him while he was in this posture, and the jinn did not discover his death, and they continued working before him, striving out of fear of him, peace be upon him.

The Truth, glorified be He, wished to end, through the death of Solomon, a matter that preoccupied the jinn and humans: the question of the jinn's knowledge of the unseen. He, glorified be He, wished to expose the jinn and show their inability to know the unseen, for the unseen is known only to God.

Solomon died standing, leaning on his staff, and remained in this state until God set a creature of the earth upon his staff, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿It was not but the creature of the earth eating away his staff that indicated to them his death...﴾ [Saba: 14].

Some understand ﴿the creature of the earth﴾ [Saba: 14] to be the creature of the earth as opposed to the heaven, but what is meant is the creature that gnaws (taqruḍ), as we say: "the mouse gnawed such and such" (qarḍ al-fa'r kadhā wa-kadhā), its verb being (qaraḍa, yaqruḍu, qarḍan), like (ḍaraba, yaḍribu, ḍarban). This creature is the woodworm that afflicts wood and eats it.

This creature, or woodworm, kept gnawing into the staff until Solomon, peace be upon him, lost his balance and fell to the ground. ﴿So when he fell, the jinn realised that if they had known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment﴾ [Saba: 14], meaning: they would not have stayed or continued in the humiliating punishment. The meaning of (kharra, "fell") is: fell without order, as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿So the roof fell upon them from above them...﴾ [al-Nahl: 26].

Thus (al-khurūr, "falling") is a collapse without order and without arrangement. At that point alone the jinn learned of Solomon's death, and so did humans, and they knew that they did not know the unseen. Had they known the unseen, they would have discovered his death, and would not have remained at work, in toil and punishment throughout this period. Then their affair was exposed, and their lie and their claim to knowledge of the unseen became known.

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿they remained not in the humiliating punishment﴾ [Saba: 14] indicates that the jinn grow tired from work, and that what befalls every living being of fatigue and exhaustion befalls them.

The (minsa'a, "staff") is the staff, from the verb (nasa'a), meaning "to delay," and the staff was called minsa'a because a person repels with it the vermin and the predatory animals that harm him, delays them away from him, drives them off, and deters them; therefore it was named minsa'a.

Our master Moses, peace be upon him, spoke about his staff when his Lord asked him: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses? He said, "It is my staff; I lean upon it, and I beat down leaves for my sheep, and I have in it other uses."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 17-18].

Moses extended his speech with God, because God made him comfortable enough to prolong it when He said to him: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 17], and did not say, for example, "What is in your hand?" Then who is it whom his Lord addresses and he does not prolong the conversation with Him, glorified and exalted be He? Nevertheless, Moses corrected himself, saying concisely: ﴿And I have in it other uses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18].

From His saying: ﴿they remained not in the humiliating punishment﴾ [Saba: 14], we understand that the work they were engaged in was arduous labour and contained humiliation for them, because the jinn think that they have superiority over humans, and that they are a kind that rose above mankind, as evidenced by the saying of their father earlier: ﴿I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ [al-A'raf: 12].

So it is humiliating for them, and a punishment, that they should be subjected to a human, work for him, and obey his command. The labour they did for Solomon, if it did not exhaust them physically, then it exhausted them psychologically, and why not, since he subjected them, one lower than them according to their assumption.

And if someone asks: how can someone who serves a prophet and associates with him be in a humiliating punishment? We say: this doubt arose from the word "jinn." We understood that all the jinn were subjected to Solomon, but the truth is that the jinn were so named because their action is hidden; we do not see it. Those who were subjected from among the jinn were the devils, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿And the devils, every builder and diver﴾ [Sad: 37].

And He said: ﴿And among the devils are those who dove for him and performed work other than that...﴾ [al-Anbiya': 82]. These are the people of the humiliating punishment, whereas the believing jinn were not subjected.

The word (kharra, "fell") meaning "fell" suggests that the dignity of a human lies in his spirit and in the secret God placed within him. Here is Solomon, the prophet of God, with his great rank and station with his Lord, of whom He says: ﴿So when he fell...﴾ [Saba: 14], as if he were an inanimate object that dropped to the ground; because when the soul departs from the body it becomes like an inanimate thing, like a staff and like a stone.

We have said before: when the soul is taken from the body, the first thing that is forgotten is its name, however great it was; they say "the corpse," then when it is placed in the coffin they say "the wood."

Glory be to God! This matter no longer has any attribute, and rather the family and loved ones hasten to be rid of it and bury it as quickly as possible, for if it remained with them no one could bear it, because of the change that befalls it and the smell from which even the closest relatives suffer.

Then the Truth, glorified be He, speaks to us about Sheba and its people, saying, exalted be He:

﴿Indeed, there was for Sheba in their dwelling a sign: two gardens on the right and on the left...﴾.

Almighty God moves us from the story of Sulayman (peace be upon him) to the people of Saba'. What is the connection between them? One who reflects on the surahs and verses of the Qur'an finds in them coherence and harmony, and the relevance here is that our master Sulayman had his most prominent story concerning matters of faith and belief with Bilqis, the queen of Saba'. There is, then, a connection between them, and this transition has its appropriateness.

The story of Sulayman, the hoopoe and Bilqis is a well-known story, and it contains great lessons of faith in belief, and in clarifying that animals have an understanding of belief and of the secrets of God in His creation.

Saba' (سَبَأ) is a proper name for a man called 'Amr ibn 'Amir, who was given the epithet Muzayqiya' (مزيقباء), and whose father was (Ma' al-sama') (water of the sky). Kurrah ibn Nusayk (may Allah be pleased with him) asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about Saba', and he said: "Such and such..." He had ten children: Azd, Kindah, Madhhij, Ash'ariyyun, Anmar, Ghassan, 'Amilah, Lakhm, Judham and Khath'am.

Each of them formed a large tribe. Six of them went to Yemen and four went to the Levant (al-Sham). Those who went to Yemen lived in its abundant good. It is related that when Bilqis saw the rainwater flowing in the valleys and being absorbed by the earth, so that they did not benefit from it, she thought of building a dam between two mountains to hold back the rainwater, and she made in it sluices like those we have in the Khayriyya barrages, for example, which open when needed and release water in measured amounts. Therefore goodness and prosperity increased in Yemen, until it was called Fertile Yemen and Happy Yemen.

However, a soothsayer among them, or a wise woman of sound opinion, said to this Saba': "The dam will be ruined and its water will flood Yemen, so leave it." Indeed Saba' left for the Hijaz and al-Sham, where the Ghassanids went to al-Sham, the Manadhira to Iraq, Anmar to Madinah, and Azd to 'Oman in Jordan.

The name Saba', after having been a proper name for a person, extended until it became the name of a tribe, and then the name of the place where they dwelt.

The words of Almighty God: ﴿There was for Saba' in their dwelling-place...﴾ [Saba': 15] mean: the place where they dwell. The place in which a person lives is called (sakan) or (bayt) or (manzil), and each of them has a meaning. The sakan is the place which a person takes in order to settle in it, find tranquillity and rest from the movement of life and work, and a person does not settle except in a place where the means of life and security are available.

Therefore, when our master Ibrahim (peace be upon him) placed his wife and son by the House, he supplicated his Lord: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in an uncultivated valley by Your Sacred House...﴾ [Ibrahim: 37].

This place was barren, with no crops and no water, and no means of life except the air. The meaning of ﴿I have settled...﴾ [Ibrahim: 37] is: I have made them settle in this place.

As for the manzil, it is the place where you alight once or several times, and then depart from it; you do not reside in it permanently. It is like the rest-stops prepared for emergencies, whose people only stay in them a few days in the whole year.

From this: sakan implies permanence and stability, while manzil is a resting place: if you wish you alight in it, and if you wish you depart from it.

As for bayt, it is associated with spending the night (al-baytutah), and a person does not sleep a restful sleep except in a place where he is safe for himself and his property, for the one who is afraid, and likewise the hungry, does not sleep.

From sakan is the words of Almighty God concerning the Children of Israel: ﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel, "Dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you forth in a mass."﴾ [al-Isra': 104].

One of the orientalists took this verse and made it an evidence that the whole earth is permissible for the Jews, since they are in the land. But when you want this matter you say: "Settle in Cairo, settle in Tanta," for example, which designates a place for me. However, ﴿dwell in the land﴾ [al-Isra': 104] has another meaning, namely the dispersal of which God said: ﴿And We divided them in the earth into communities...﴾ [al-A'raf: 168].

That is: they have no specific homeland, and they will spread throughout the whole world, and no one will be able to strike them or destroy them while they are in this state of dispersal, until the command of God comes and gathers them in one place, and then it will be easy to destroy them.

The meaning of the word ﴿sign (āyah)...﴾ [Saba': 15]: we say, "So-and-so is a sign in generosity, and so-and-so is a sign in courtesy," etc., and what is meant is a wonderful thing of rare existence. Almighty God has told us of three kinds of signs: cosmic signs, such as: ﴿And of His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon...﴾ [Fussilat: 37] ﴿And of His signs is that you see the earth humbled, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells...﴾ [Fussilat: 39].

And signs in the sense of miracles and things beyond custom, which come at the hands of the messengers to confirm them and establish the truth of their conveyance from God, as in His words: ﴿Insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without harm...﴾ [al-Qasas: 32].

Then the signs are applied to the verses of the Book bearing God's rulings in the noble Qur'an. All of these—whether cosmic signs, miracles, or verses of the Qur'an—are all wonders, and although these wonders are evident in cosmic signs and in miracles, they are also evident in the verses of the Wise Book. The Qur'an is a wonder in organizing people's lives, as evidenced by the fact that the unbeliever in it will be compelled to adopt its rulings and submit to its laws, not as a religion, but as laws of life.

We have previously given an example of this with the rulings on divorce, which they have often criticized and attacked, accusing the religion of God—wrongly and ignorantly—of harshness; then afterwards we see them resorting to it, and finding no solution to some of their problems except in divorce and in returning to the rulings of God, although they do not believe in Him. This is the utmost victory of the religion of God, that the unbeliever in it returns to it. It is the victory of truth and the victory of proof.

We have also said previously that one of the orientalists asked us in San Francisco, saying: In the Qur'an is ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion, even if the polytheists dislike it﴾ [al-Saff: 9].

"After fourteen centuries, Judaism, Christianity, Buddhism... etc. still exist in the world." This statement shows a lack of understanding of the meaning of the verses, for what is meant by ﴿to make it prevail over all religion...﴾ [al-Saff: 9] is not that all people become believers, as evidenced by His words ﴿even if the polytheists dislike it...﴾ [al-Saff: 9].

Therefore: the religion will prevail with the prevalence of proof and the prevalence of dominance over their legislations, and there will befall them of the problems of life what they cannot find a solution for except in the Law of God. This is the prevalence intended in the verse.

Then Almighty God clarifies the nature of the sign that Saba' had in their dwelling-place, saying: ﴿Two gardens on the right and on the left...﴾ [Saba': 15]. Since God the Exalted described these two gardens as a sign, there must be wonders in them, and they differ from the gardens that we know.

The scholars have told us about these wonders, saying of these two gardens: you will not find in them a scorpion, nor a snake, nor a fly, nor a flea, etc. If some visitor came to them with lice on his body, he would die merely by entering one of these two gardens. All these are wonders of the two gardens.

We note here that the word "sign" is singular while the wonders are many, because the word āyah is also applied to the plural. Of this is the words of Almighty God concerning our master 'Isa (peace be upon him): ﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign...﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50], and He did not say "two signs." They said: because the wondrous matter that united them is one: 'Isa (peace be upon him) was born without a male, and his mother conceived and gave birth likewise without a male, so the two are one sign.

The meaning of ﴿two gardens on the right and on the left...﴾ [Saba': 15] may be that each of them has two gardens, one on the right and the other on the left, with his house in the middle; and it may be that the two gardens belong to the people of Saba' all together, meaning that they are gardens connected on the right and gardens connected on the left, joined without being separated by walls or fences, which indicates that security was established among them. We have witnessed something similar in America, where the fields and farms extend connected, separated only by a simple wire.

As for His words, glory be to Him: ﴿Eat of the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him...﴾ [Saba': 15]. How do we understand ﴿Eat of the provision of your Lord...﴾ [Saba': 15], when all people eat from the provision of God? They said: people eat from the provision of God through means; but this is the provision of God directly, without means. Therefore He says in another place: ﴿Eat of the good things that We have provided for you...﴾ [Ta-Ha: 81].

Not all provision is good to eat; rather here ﴿Eat of the provision of your Lord...﴾ [Saba': 15] means that all of it is good and all of it is sweet. The fruit in these two gardens does not suffer blight, and no corruption befalls their fruits as befalls fruit elsewhere; therefore He, glory be to Him, will say at the end of the verse: ﴿A good land and a Forgiving Lord﴾ [Saba': 15].

We know that the labour required in gardens is little; therefore we see the farmer, when working the land and wages become burdensome, resorts to planting gardens and fruitful orchards, because they cost less and do not need much care except at the time of fruiting.

Almighty God says in another place: ﴿Have you considered what you sow? Is it you who cultivate it, or are We the cultivators?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 63-64], so He affirmed for them work and tillage. But the matter here concerns these two gardens, which are a gift from God without work and without means. So God, glory be to Him, is the sower, and He has given it a gentle atmosphere, neither heat nor cold, nor weariness, nor fear, nor indifference to any blessing through its repetition.

Thus there is no work for them in their gardens that produces what they enjoy; rather their work is to thank the Bestower, glory be to Him, that He may increase them in goodness, and gratitude for blessings is the wisdom of the servant with his Master. Therefore He, glory be to Him, said about Luqman: ﴿And We certainly gave Luqman wisdom...﴾ [Luqman: 12]. What was this wisdom? ﴿That give thanks to Allah...﴾ [Luqman: 12], because thanks for a blessing increases it.

His words, glory be to Him: ﴿A good land...﴾ [Saba': 15] mean: it gives you the best of things without any troubles in them; for there are things that give you a goodness you enjoy, but they tire you and trouble you afterwards.

As for this land, there is nothing in it that you eat with ease and pleasure, for it is the provision of God without means from the servants. But when the servants interfere in God's bounty, troubles and vexations appear in the blessings. This is what we suffer from now, through interference with crops by chemical materials and insecticides, which have ruined our lives, and whose harm has exceeded their benefit, until we attribute all diseases to our interference in God's bounty. If we had left the land to be watered by the rain of the sky as it was at the beginning, we would have tasted goodness without vexations. It is therefore necessary that we show proper manners toward God in His bounty.

Therefore you will find that many of the affluent, the intellectuals, the people of knowledge and the philosophers love to leave the noise of cities, the pollution of their air and water, and their clamour, and go out to the countryside or the wilderness, fleeing from the harmful effects of modern civilization into the open, where the shepherd lives, where nature is as God created it, and where the sound disposition is found that man has not interfered with.

You remember in the past, we used to combat the cotton worm by natural manual methods. When sciences advanced, they brought the substance (DDT) to eliminate the cotton worm, but this poisonous substance killed everything in the fields, destroyed the fish in the canals and drains, destroyed the (abu qurdan) bird, the farmer's friend, and polluted the water and the crops, etc. As for the cotton worm, it alone developed immunity, and became, as we have said, "immune" to DDT.

As for Saba', it was ﴿a good land﴾ [Saba': 15], with all its goodness of water, air and soil; no pollution of any kind had touched it. And if the land itself is good, what then of what is upon it?

In the verse there are two commands: ﴿Eat of the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him...﴾ [Saba': 15], and in it is a warning: beware of being deceived by the blessing and thinking that it has become your property, forgetting the Bestower of it upon you. Beware of being like the one of whom God said: ﴿Nay! Indeed, man does transgress, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-'Alaq: 6-7].

Beware of thinking that you are the originator in this matter; remain always mindful that the Bestower is God, and that what you are in is from the gift of God, and then you must thank Him, glory be to Him, for gratitude binds blessings.

In another place, Almighty God spoke of thanking for blessings, saying: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba': 13]. Praise be to God that He, glory be to Him, did not say "and few of My servants are the grateful" (singular). You know that shakur is an intensive form of shukr, or that the shakur is the one who thanks for a blessing and then thanks God for having inspired him to give thanks for the blessing, as if he has offered thanks twice.

Then He did not confine the blessing to the people of Saba' in this world alone; rather His blessing upon them extended to the Hereafter. In this world: ﴿a good land﴾ [Saba': 15], and in the Hereafter: ﴿and a Forgiving Lord﴾ [Saba': 15], meaning: He will overlook it for you if a slip or a lapse occurs from you.

Then Almighty God makes clear the outcome and their response, saying:

﴿But they turned away, so We sent upon them the flood of al-'Arim...﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 34, verse 16:

Allah's words: ﴿So they turned away﴾. That is, from what they were commanded, which is ﴿Eat of the provision of your Lord and give thanks to Him﴾ [Saba': 15]. So they did not eat from the provision of Allah; rather they ate from their own effort and skill, according to their own claim. This is the first of the losses. Then they did not thank Allah for these blessings, because the blessings made them affluent (atrafathum), so they forgot to be grateful for them.

There is a difference between taraf and atraf. We say: taraf so-and-so, meaning he lived in luxury and comfort. But atraf so-and-so means the blessing deceived him (ghharathu al-ni'mah). Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones (mutrafiha), and they commit wickedness therein﴾ [al-Isra': 16].

So there is no harm in enjoying comfort, but the calamity is that blessing makes you tyrannical and deceives you. The first form of tyranny through blessing is that you attribute it to yourself and say: "By my effort and my cleverness," like the one who said: ﴿I was only given it on account of knowledge I have﴾ [al-Qasas: 78]. Then you forget the Benefactor and do not thank Him for the blessing...

The word i'rad (turning away) gives something beyond neglect and beyond forgetfulness, because i'rad is to turn away from the one who addresses you and to give him your side...

So: i'rad is a deliberate abandonment with indifference. As for inadvertence (sahw), forgetfulness (nisyan), error (khata'), or while sleeping, these are all matters pardoned, which Allah has lifted from us out of mercy toward us. Your Lord, Mighty and Majestic, deals with you only on the basis of wakefulness, attentiveness, and deliberate action.

And if you wish, read your Lord's saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed he will have a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ [Ta-Ha: 124].

Why? Because i'rad involves an appearance of not caring about the one who commands, so the calamity in it is greater than if you were attentive to the commander; and afterward you blame yourself for some other cause...

So what was the result of this turning away? He, exalted is He, says: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood of the dam (sayl al-'Arim)﴾. That is, after the Dam of Ma'rib (sadd al-'Arim) collapsed, its water flowed and drowned them. And it is remarkable that Allah, exalted is He, made from water every living thing [al-Anbiya': 30], but when He wills it as a means of destruction, He destroys; and with it Allah destroyed the people of Noah, and with it He destroyed Pharaoh and his hosts. This is from the absoluteness of Allah's power, as He directs a thing to life so it lives, and to destruction so it destroys.

And after the flood of al-'Arim terrified them, why did they wish to settle afterward? They settled in places where there was no water; when they wanted water, they brought it from wells in water-skins (qirab), and it is as if water had created in them a complex ('uqdah)...

As for sayl (flood): it is when water flows over the surface of the earth after the earth has absorbed from it its needed amount, so what overflows over it flows from one place to another. The Truthful, exalted is He, teaches us: before we search for the sources of water, we must search for its outlets, so that it does not drown us...

Then the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, affirms that what befell them was not an injustice done to them; rather, it was the recompense for what they did. That is: what was mentioned before, the bitter-fruited tree (al-khamt), the tamarisk (al-athl) and the lote tree (al-sidr), "We recompensed them" — that is, as a requital for them, "for their disbelief" (bi-ma kafaru). Kufr (disbelief) is the concealment of blessing, and these people concealed the blessing of God when they thought that they were eating from their own toil, their striving and their possessions, and they concealed the blessing of God when they did not turn to the Bestower, glorified is He, and did not give Him thanks. So they did not obey Him in ﴿Eat of the provision of your Lord﴾ [Saba': 15], nor in ﴿and give thanks to Him﴾ [Saba': 15].

Then the Truth, glorified is He, declares His own transcendence through this rhetorical interrogative: ﴿And do We recompense any but the ungrateful?﴾ He used the word al-kafur, which is an intensive form (sigha mubalagha), and He did not say al-kafir (the disbeliever). This is from His mercy toward His servants: He recompenses from them only the al-kafur, that is, the one who persists in disbelief and persists in it relentlessly.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 34, verse 18:

We know that the people of Yemen were merchants engaged in trade between Yemen and al-Sham (Greater Syria). God made for them, along the route of their trade, ﴿قُرًى ظَاهِرَةً﴾ (manifest towns). That is: close together and continuous, serving as resting-places along the road... This was because of the great distance between Yemen and al-Sham... So the Truth, glorified is He, wished to make those journeys easy for them, and to cover them without hardship.

﴿وَقَدَّرْنَا فِيهَا السَّيْرَ﴾ (And We measured therein the travel). That is: We made their travel over close distances, so the manifest towns were for them on their journey and near to them, such that they pass by them and see them on their way without hardship: towns distributed along the stages of the road, so that whenever they travelled a distance, they found a town on the main route.

This means that they would be safe, nothing frightening them, and that they would not need to carry provisions, since the towns they passed would suffice them for the needs of the road, and they would find what they required there. This also means that they would not need many beasts for carrying loads.

And al-Sayr (the travel) means in the morning; it is also said of the morning and the evening journey. Then the Truth, glorified is He, gives them companionship in this matter: ﴿سِيرُوا فِيهَا لَيَالِيَ وَأَيَّامًا آمِنِينَ﴾ (Travel therein, nights and days, in security). So that they travel in the morning to a place where they rest at midday, and travel in the evening to a place where they spend the night. That is: a station for the midday rest and a station for the night's lodging. This travel was under a shade of security and safety which the Truth, glorified is He, guaranteed for them, so nothing terrifies them, neither from people nor from wild beasts.

When we compare His saying here, ﴿آمِنِينَ﴾ (secure), with His saying, exalted is He, about Quraysh: ﴿الَّذِي أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍ وَآمَنَهُم مِّنْ خَوْفٍ﴾ [Quraysh: 4] (Who fed them against hunger and made them secure against fear), we find that security is attained through feeding and safety from fear. Here He said ﴿آمِنِينَ﴾ and did not say "from fear," because the meaning of ﴿آمِنِينَ﴾ [Saba': 18] is complete security: secure from fear and secure from hunger, since no complement was mentioned with ﴿آمِنِينَ﴾ [Saba': 18].

Consider this obstinacy and this ingratitude for God's blessing: they were not pleased that God had made the towns close to one another for them, so they said, "Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys farther apart" — that is, separate these towns with vast deserts, such that none can travel through them except the wealthy and capable who own strong mounts able to carry loads.

So their outlook on this matter is wholly economic, full of greed and covetousness. They wanted to deprive the poor and those unable to travel of trading with them. When the towns are close together and the resting places along the road are numerous, a traveler scarcely passes one town before the next appears to him from afar. This makes travel easy for the poor who ride weak beasts, for means of riding differ according to people's capabilities: one rides a thoroughbred horse, another a she-camel, and another a donkey.

The nearness of distances between the towns encouraged the poor to set out on the journey to the Levant (al-Sham); therefore these people asked that God put distance between these towns. It is a greedy, selfish demand. Hence God, Exalted, said after it: ﴿And they wronged themselves﴾. Indeed, they wronged themselves, for they deprived themselves of the ease that God had provided for them, and they wronged themselves because they wanted to monopolize this trade and prevent others, the poor among them, from going out to it. Or they wronged themselves because they demonstrated for themselves the incompleteness of faith, since faith is not complete for a believer until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself, whereas these people love to monopolize the blessing for themselves and deprive others of it.

But how could the distancing they requested be realized along the route of their trade? We know from the science of geometry that the straight line is the shortest distance between two points, so a straight road facilitates movement along it and reduces time and effort. Distancing could only be achieved by destroying some of the towns so as to lengthen the distance between them, or by having the road wind and turn here and there.

The result of this greed and ingratitude was ﴿So We made them into tales, and tore them apart completely﴾. That is: a legend that people speak of, or a story that is recounted, just as when a criminal falls into the hands of the police, and they make him an example for others until people tell tales of him. Likewise, the people of Saba' became an example for others by God, until their story became a proverb struck. In the Arabic proverb expressing dispersion they say: "They scattered like the hands of Saba'," meaning: they dispersed after being gathered, just as the people of Saba' were scattered.

The meaning of ﴿and tore them apart completely﴾ is: tearing and dispersing in every kind and manner, such that the tearing encompasses every part, however small.

﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾: that is, there are lessons and admonitions in it from which the intelligent person benefits in his life.

﴿For every steadfast, grateful person﴾. "Steadfast" (ṣabbār) and "grateful" (shakūr) are intensive forms. Ṣabbār is an intensive form from ṣabr (patience), because these people oppressed and persecuted the poor and wanted to cut off the path of blessing for them and monopolize it for themselves, and this conduct recurred from them. Therefore it does not say "every patient person" (ṣābir), for they endured such harm that much patience was required.

He also said shakūr, meaning: one who is much thankful to God for enabling him to be patient...

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 34, verse 20:

The meaning of ﴿And certainly﴾ [Saba': 20]: emphasis, once with the lam and once with qad. ﴿Proved true﴾ [Saba': 20]: confirmed and affirmed. ﴿Concerning them﴾ [Saba': 20]: concerning the people of Saba' and those like them who followed him. ﴿Iblis, his supposition﴾ [Saba': 20]: What was Iblis's supposition? His supposition was that human desires would enable him to lead them astray. We know his story when God commanded him to prostrate to Adam, and he refused and said in threat: ﴿Because You have sent me astray, I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ [al-A'raf: 16]. He also said: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82]. But there still remained in him some shame, so he said: ﴿except Your chosen servants among them﴾ [al-Hijr: 40].

So Iblis's supposition was as if he said: "I have led their father astray, and I had power over him when I misled him. He ate from the tree although he was the first of creation and the strongest of them, and God had charged him directly with only one thing, namely that he should eat from all the fruits of Paradise except this tree. Yet I had power over him. Therefore I have power over his offspring, because they are weaker than he is, and God has charged them indirectly, with many obligations. So I have more power over them than I had over their father."

This supposition of Iblis was not knowledge of the unseen; rather, it was an analogy by which he measured the descendants of Adam against their father. If Adam was the first creature whom God created with His own hand, whose angels He made prostrate to him, whom He charged directly and charged with only one matter, and yet I had power over him, then I have even more power over his descendants. This is an analogy that Iblis did not reach through authority or honour; therefore it was called a supposition.

When Iblis had power over the descendants of Adam and actually led them astray, he said: "My supposition came true in its proper place, for they indeed followed him." ﴿And Iblis certainly proved true his supposition concerning them, and they followed him, except a party of the believers﴾ [Saba': 20]. Then this exception comes: ﴿except a party of the believers﴾ [Saba': 20], so this exception corresponds to the first exception: ﴿except Your chosen servants among them﴾ [al-Hijr: 40].

Then the Truthful, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And he had no authority over them, except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it...﴾.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 34, verse 21:

When Iblis misled the children of Adam, do they have an excuse for this misleading? And is the sin here Iblis's sin? God, exalted is He, reports this about him and about them in the context of the story of Saba': ﴿He had no authority over them...﴾ [Saba': 21]. Iblis seized upon this phrase and made it a proof for himself on the Day of Resurrection. When humankind says to him on the Day of Resurrection, "You are the cause of our misguidance and our going astray," he says: ﴿I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves...﴾ [Ibrahim: 22].

That is, "Do not blame me and do not wrong me. You were under my sway, and I had no authority over you: no authority of force by which I could subdue you and compel you to obey me, and no authority of proof by which I could convince you. The difference between the authority of force and the authority of proof is that with the first you act while unwilling, so you are coerced, whereas with the authority of proof and reason you do what is asked of you willingly and with conviction."

Our Lord, mighty and majestic, has warned us against Iblis, his whispering and his prodding, and taught us that we cannot overcome him except through God, especially by this "prescription" in which God said: ﴿And if a prodding from Satan should touch you, then seek refuge in God...﴾ [Fussilat: 36].

Merely by mentioning God to him, he shrinks back, flees and retreats. He has power over you alone, but if you turn to your Lord he is frightened and flees, because he has no power and no scheme in the presence of the remembrance of God. For this reason some of the knowers of God said: "Say this word forcefully, as if you see him and are throwing him down."

So what should one of us do if this comes upon him while he is reciting the Qur'an? They said: he should stop his recitation and say, in a louder voice and in a different manner from his recitation: "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan." We have tried to bring this meaning closer to the minds of the young, saying: if, for example, a wealthy man is sitting on his balcony at night and sees a thief trying to enter his house, he rises from his place and says "ahem." What does the thief do? He flees. If he says to himself, "Perhaps it was a coincidence," and then returns the next night, the owner of the house is alerted to him and says "ahem" again, and then the thief flees without returning, because the owner of the house is awake and not heedless.

Likewise, the saying "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan" frightens Satan and drives him away. If he returns to you again and again, then say, every time you feel his whispering and prodding: "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan." Then he will know that you have "cracked" him, and that he has no way into you.

Iblis, when he argued with his Lord, knew from where he would enter upon the children of Adam, and he said: ﴿I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path﴾ [al-A'raf: 16]. As we have mentioned, he does not sit in a tavern, for example; rather he sits in the mosque. He knows that you are in worship, and his whole aim is to spoil your worship for you. Do you not see how he reminds you, during prayer, of the important matters of life that you had forgotten? The believer must regard his standing before God and must not occupy himself with anything while in the presence of his Lord.

So prayer is the straight path upon which Satan will lie in wait for you. For this reason our jurists, may God have mercy on them and be pleased with them, taught us to enrage Satan: if he whispers to you in prayer so that you do not know whether you have prayed two or three rak'ahs, then count it as two and build upon the minimum. Likewise in ablution and similar acts of worship, so that you enrage him and make him despair of you.

The phenomenon of forgetfulness in prayer is in reality a healthy phenomenon, for it is [a sign of] faith. So do not make yourself ill with it. Be strong in faith and be bold against this enemy, and say to him: "I will not give you the opportunity to spoil my meeting with my Lord." Say this with a surge of faith, and you will burn him. If he returns, then return [to the same response]. And know that the scheme of Satan is weak: ﴿Indeed, the scheme of Satan is ever weak﴾ [al-Nisa': 76].

He has no power over you as long as you are in God's company and as long as you are remembering God. With you is an awakening of faith and an awakening of creed.

We have previously recounted the story of Imam Abu Hanifa, when a man came to him asking for a fatwa and said: "O Imam, I had hidden some money in a place in the desert and marked it with a stone, but a flood came and obliterated it, so I lost the exact spot." The Imam laughed and, with his experience, expertise and faculty for giving fatwas, said to the man: "My son, there is no knowledge of this, but I will devise a stratagem for you. Go after you have prayed the 'isha' prayer, perform a fresh ablution with the intention that God guide you to what you have lost, pray two rak'ahs to God, and then tell me what happens."

The man did what the Imam instructed. Iblis came to him to spoil his prayer and said: "The money is in such-and-such a place." So he went and found the money, then returned to the Imam and informed him. The Imam said: "By God, I knew that Satan would not let you complete your night with your Lord."

So: trust in the phrase "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan," and say it with the strength of faith. Would God utter a word that comes into the reality of life from a believer in Him, only for that believer to make it a lie? Try it yourself.

As for His exalted saying: ﴿...except that We might know who believes in the Hereafter from one who is in doubt about it...﴾ [Saba': 21]: since Iblis has no authority over the children of Adam, and since they are under his sway, their faith must not be firmly rooted, and they must have forgotten one of God's rulings, since He warned them against him and described to them the way to overcome him, yet they did not act upon it.

Thus Iblis's misleading of them was ﴿that We might know who believes in the Hereafter from one who is in doubt about it...﴾ [Saba': 21], meaning: knowledge of occurrence. Otherwise, God, exalted is He, knows from eternity what will come from them; but the act must actually take place from them so that the proof may be established against them. This is like the teacher who sees signs of failure in his student and warns him. When the student enters the examination and fails, he comes to complain to his teacher that he had foretold his failure, and the teacher says: "Did I hold your hand and prevent you from answering? I judged you by the preliminary signs I saw in you."

Nevertheless, it was possible that this student could cheat in the examination and pass despite what the teacher said, because the teacher's knowledge is incomplete, whereas the knowledge of the Truth, exalted is He, is complete. So knowledge of occurrence is more binding as proof.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And your Lord is over all things Hafiz﴾ [Saba': 21]. Ḥafīẓ (حفيظ) is an intensive form (sigha mubālagha) derived from ḥifẓ (الحفظ), "preservation." So God is Ḥafīẓ over treasures, over provisions, over knowledge and over everything, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿And there is nothing but that with Us are its stores, and We send it down only in a known measure﴾ [al-Hijr: 21]. And since God is the Ḥafīẓ, no one can disrupt this matter.

Then the Truth, exalted is He, says:

﴿Say: Call upon those you claim besides God...﴾.

The Almighty moves on to a general matter: the case of those people who worship other than God, and He argues with them to show the corruption of their path and the falsity of their worship apart from God. They replied with this:

﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us nearer to God in closeness﴾ [Az-Zumar: 3].

First, we say: what is worship? Worship is that the worshipper obeys the command and prohibition of the one worshipped. So if the disbelievers worship the sun, the moon, or idols, and so on, what have these deities commanded them? And from what have they forbidden them? What reward have these deities prepared for those who worship them? And what punishment have they prepared for those who disbelieve in them?

So: you are lying in your saying "we worship them." If you worship them so that they may bring you near to God in closeness, then why do you not direct your worship to God directly? How can you worship gods that have no method and no action toward those who worship them, and no action toward those who disbelieve in their worship?

These creatures that they worship besides God are created by God, subjected to Him, glorifying Him. They are innocent of this association (shirk) and do not approve of it. Rather, they are more devoted in worship to God than they are. Therefore the stones spoke on the tongue of this poet, and they said:

Then the Almighty debates them on this matter: ﴿Say: Call upon those you claimed besides God﴾. Call upon these supposed deities. But they did not call upon them, because they knew that their alleged gods would not answer. So God completed the argument for them and showed them the outcome: if you called upon these deities, they would not possess ﴿an atom's weight in the heavens or in the earth﴾...

So for what then do you worship them, when they possess nothing, have done you no kindness, and have offered you no service? ﴿And they have no share in them﴾, that is, in the heavens and the earth, ﴿of partnership﴾, meaning: with God; that is, they have no partnership with God in the matter of creation. ﴿And He has no supporter among them﴾, meaning: they did not help God when He created the heavens and the earth. The ẓahīr (supporter) is the strong helper...

When sound human nature and natural religiosity collide with the desires of the soul, a person seeks a religion that satisfies his desires and fulfills his instincts. He wants to be religious, and at the same time he wants his desires not to be restricted. So what does he do? He resorts to worshipping gods with no method and no obligations. From here people worshipped other than God. Leave aside those who worshipped trees and stones, and consider those who worshipped the angels, for example: did they command them anything, or forbid them anything?

Therefore the Almighty says: ﴿Say: Call upon those you claimed besides God﴾. If we examine the matter of partners by reason, its falsehood and untruth become evident. If God, exalted is He, has partners, and there are other gods with Him, then where are they? Did they know that God has monopolized divinity, testified to it for Himself, and declared it explicitly without them? If they knew of that, why did they leave Him to monopolize divinity? And if they did not know of that, then they are sleeping gods? In both cases they do not deserve this divinity.

Therefore the Almighty addresses this matter with beauty, saying:

﴿Say: If there were with Him other gods, as they say, then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾ [Al-Isra: 42]. That is: if it were true that there are gods with God, they would have gone to Him to contend with Him, asking why He monopolized divinity to the exclusion of them; or they would have gone to Him to fear Him and to draw near to Him.

The most elevated objects of worship among the polytheists are the angels, as if their worship had become close to the worship of God. And God says about the angels:

﴿Rather, they are honoured servants. They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 26-27].

And the Qur'an answers them:

﴿Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means of access to their Lord, which of them is nearest, and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment﴾ [Al-Isra: 57].

So these angels whom you worship besides God are themselves seeking nearness to God and seeking means of access to Him. The nearest of them seeks a means to God, and loves to be nearer still. If the nearest is the one who seeks the means and nearness, then what about the one who is near? And what about the distant and the more distant?

So: you are foolish in worshipping the angels. Do you think that a creature of God's creation, such as the angels, would be content that you worship them besides God, or would accept to intercede for you with God? This is foolishness in thinking.

The Almighty has set conditions for intercession, so He says:

﴿On that Day, intercession will not benefit except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted and whose word He approves﴾ [Ta-Ha: 109].

Scholars have said: intercession requires a condition regarding the one for whom intercession is sought, namely that he be among the people of tawhid (monotheism), and a condition regarding the intercessor, namely that he be permitted to intercede, as the Exalted said:

﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. So the intercessor does not rise and intercede directly; rather he waits to be given permission to do so. At this point the one for whom intercession is sought becomes agitated and terrified, anxious, wondering: will the intercessor be permitted, or will his intercession be rejected?

Therefore the Exalted says: ﴿until, when the terror is removed from their hearts...﴾ meaning: the terror is removed from them. The intensive form in (fuzzi'a) indicates the removal of the state derived from the verb...

﴿They say, "What has your Lord said?" They say, "The truth."﴾ That is, He said the true word and permitted intercession for whomever He is pleased with.

And the Exalted said: ﴿nor will intercession benefit...﴾ and He did not say "intercession will not be accepted," because the aim of the intercessor is that the intercession benefit the one for whom it is sought. When he goes to intercede for him, the one with whom intercession is made says to him: "I am not pleased that you intercede for the one for whom you intercede." What is negated is the benefit of intercession, not its acceptance. Thus there is a difference between intercession occurring and intercession benefiting...

It is called shafa'ah (intercession) because the shaf' (even) is the opposite of the watr (odd). The person in need who seeks intercession is one; when the intercessor joins him, they become two, i.e., shaf' (a pair).

Then He, glory be to Him, says at the close of the verse: ﴿and He is the Most High, the Great﴾ [Saba': 23]. Most High, so that no decision He makes can be questioned; and Great, meaning greater than the intercessor and greater than the one for whom intercession is sought. The Truth, glory be to Him, spoke the truth and uttered it, which means that He stood by the truth; He paid no heed to any intercessor, however high his rank, nor to any one seeking intercession, however lowly his humiliation and weakness, because He, glory be to Him, is the Most High, the Great.

After that, the Truth, glory be to Him, returns to discussing the matter through rational argument, saying:

﴿Say, "Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?" Say, "Allah."...﴾

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 34, verse 24:

That is: say to them, O Muhammad: who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? But if Muhammad is the one who asks them, who will answer? Of course they will not answer; so God answers (Say: "God"). This is a fact they cannot confront, and if they acknowledged it, we would then say to them: why, then, do you not believe in God, since He is your provider?

Is it fitting for you to disbelieve in Him while He is the Provider, and to believe in other gods that neither benefit you nor harm you? Their acknowledgment of this fact binds them to the proof and establishes the evidence against the foolishness of their thinking. It is as if the Truthful, glorified is He, wished to spare them this embarrassment, so He answered in their place.

God, glorified and exalted, asks them this question because the answer can only be in accordance with His will, glorified and exalted be He...

And His saying, glorified and exalted be He: "And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error."

Guidance (al-huda) is indication toward good and the path to it, and error (al-dalal) is that you go astray from good and from the indication toward it. Among its uses is His saying, exalted be He: "And He found you lost and guided you" [al-Duha: 7].

Guidance and error are among the contradictories (al-mutanaqidan) in religion, and two contradictories never come together. Thus one of them must be upon guidance and the other upon error. Many people do not understand the difference between the opposite (al-did) and the contradictory (al-naqid). The opposite is something that opposes another thing but does not negate it, as when you say, for example: is such-and-such thing red or green? And he says to you: neither red nor green, but white. So two opposites do not come together, and they may both be absent together, neither this nor that, but something else. As for contradictories, if one is removed, the other is established, as here with guidance and error.

So the meaning of "And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error" is: if one of us is upon guidance, the other must be in error, and there is no third. The discussion here concerns a sound method on the side of faith and an evil method on the side of disbelief. The Messenger of God says to them: we and you are on opposite sides. We say "There is no god but God" and call to good, while you disbelieve in God and call to evil. Yet he does not rule in his own favour that he is upon guidance, nor rule against you that you are in error; rather he says: I and you are opposites; if one of us is upon guidance, the other is in error.

By God, have you seen argument gentler than this argument? The Messenger of God did not rule for himself and the believers with him that they were upon guidance, despite its clarity on their side, nor did he rule against the disbelievers that they were in error, despite its clarity on their side. An example of this: if two men swear to one thing before a blind man, would he say to one, "You are truthful," and to the other, "You are lying"? No, he says: one of you is truthful and the other is lying. This is a preliminary judgment that binds no one.

But when the matter is examined, it becomes clear to you who is upon guidance and who is in clear error. "And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error." The word 'alā (upon) in "upon guidance" indicates elevation, as if guidance does not rise above you, but rather you rise above guidance and are higher than it, as if it were a mount that conveys you to the desired good and the straight path. So when you read ('alā), know that there is a high place, and there is what is below this...

So we say: "upon guidance," meaning: guidance will be your mount that conveys you to Paradise and to bliss. As for error, He said "in error," as if it were a darkness surrounding the one who has gone astray, in which he flounders, not knowing where to go. And the meaning of "clear" (mubin) is evident and manifest.

This is another display of gentleness and a rise in the argument with the disbelievers, showing how keen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was to remove resentment from the hearts of the disbelievers. Consider: ﴿You will not be asked about what we committed of crime﴾. Here the Messenger of Allah attributes the crime to his own side, and this time he does not equate the two parties as he did there, when He said ﴿Indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24]. Rather, he described his own action as a crime, and said of the disbelievers ﴿And we will not be asked about what you do﴾, and did not say "what you commit as crimes."

There is another subtle point in the verse: the use of ﴿أَجْرَمْنَا﴾ (ajramna, "we committed a crime") in the past tense, as though the crime had already occurred, whereas the verb ﴿تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (ta'lamun, "you do") is in the present tense, to indicate that it has not yet happened from them. This is another gentleness, a rise in the discussion, and an endearment toward the opponent, perhaps he will turn back, so that Allah rejoices in his repentance and his return to His vast mercy.

This style of disputation in the two verses is only possible from a debater of strong proof, one whom no earlier slip from his opponent can dislodge from it. Similar to this is our saying in debate: "Let us grant for the sake of argument such-and-such," and we content ourselves with the lesser, why? Because you know that you are upon the truth, and the strength of your argument makes you confident that the investigation of the matter will end in your favour.

Yet, despite this, how does the Truth, glorified is He, command His Prophet (ﷺ) to attribute the crime to himself? They said: because the offence differs according to the one addressed by it, as they said: "The good deeds of the righteous are sins for those brought near."

Then the verses conclude with the summary of this matter in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Say: Our Lord will gather us together, then He will judge between us with truth....﴾

The meaning: We will not prolong the debate and argument with you, because we speak the truth while you toy with falsehood. The conclusion with you is that God will judge between us and you in His divine court. ﴿Say: Our Lord will gather us together﴾ — that is, on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Then He will open up between us with truth﴾ — that is, He will judge and decide. In some of our lands, even until now, they call the judge "al-Fattah" (the Opener). ﴿And He is the Opener, the All-Knowing﴾ — that is, the One who judges with complete knowledge, from whom nothing is hidden.

The judgment is called "fath" (opening) because it opens one thing from another and creates a gap between them. It is as though the two were intertwined, such that truth becomes confused with falsehood, and as though it were a battle. Then the judgment comes and unties this entanglement, and untying this entanglement is the "fath." Nothing opens between truth and falsehood except God.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 34, verse 27:

The Almighty commands His Prophet (ﷺ): "Say to them: Show me those whom you have joined with Allah as partners." He (ﷺ) already sees them in actuality; he sees their idols which they worship besides Allah. So what is the purpose of "أَرُونِيَ" ("show me")? It is said: because when he makes this demand of them, he knows that they are too ashamed to point to them, and they do not dare to do so, because they know that they are deaf stones, which neither harm nor benefit.

The meaning of أَلْحَقْتُمْ بِهِ شُرَكَآءَ ("you have joined to Him partners") is from ilhaq (attaching), which is to bring something new and attach it to something established. It is as if the divinity of Allah is the established, true divinity, and their new gods are an incidental addition to it, not original. Faith is established, original and innate in the human soul, whereas these gods are newly invented, incidental and false. Therefore He negates them with His saying: "Nay..." (كَلاَّ).

Then this preceding statement is set aside in order to establish divinity for Allah alone: "Nay, He is Allah, the Almighty, the Wise" (بَلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ). The particle "بل" (bal, "nay/rather") indicates the turning away from what precedes it and the affirmation of the ruling for what follows it: the true God is Allah.

His saying "بَلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ" ("Nay, He is Allah") also comes here with the third-person pronoun "هُوَ" (huwa, "He"). It is well known that a third-person pronoun does not come unless it is preceded by a referent. You say: "A man came to me, so I honored him" (جاءني على فأكرمتُه). But with Allah, the Exalted, the pronoun "هو" precedes its referent: "Nay, He is Allah." Why? We have said: because it is a pronoun that refers to no one but a single absent being, the Supreme Existent, glorified is He.

Then the Almighty says:

﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾

Their meaning: *"We have not sent you"*, that is, We made you a messenger, *"except comprehensively to mankind"*. The word *kāffah* (comprehensively, all-encompassing) shows the rank of the Seal of the Messengers. Before the mission of our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), a messenger was sent to specific peoples, as He, glorified and exalted, said: *"And [He will make him] a messenger to the Children of Israel: 'Indeed, I have come to you with a sign from your Lord...'"* (Al 'Imran: 49).

That is because when mankind multiplied, as He, glorified, said: *"And from both of them He spread many men and women"* (An-Nisa': 1), they scattered throughout the corners of the earth, here and there, while the world was still in the childhood of its natural state. There were no advances that would bring these groups together, so they were isolated communities with no connection between them, and each environment had its own diseases. Some cheated in measure and weight, and others worshipped idols, etc. So a messenger would come to a specific people to treat their disease, having no relation to others.

As for our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he was the Seal of the Messengers, sent to people comprehensively, because God, exalted, knew from eternity that the world would come to a meeting point, and that there would be connection between the communities that had been scattered. Today we live in a "global village," where what happens in the farthest parts of the world we hear and see at the time it happens. And since the world's societies and continents have come together, the diseases are one; therefore one messenger came to treat all diseases in all societies. This is the meaning of: *"And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind"* (Saba': 28).

The meaning of his, (ﷺ), being the Seal of the Messengers is that he is witnessed to, and is not a witness for others. God, exalted, took a covenant from the messengers that when Muhammad comes they would bear witness to him, and they all bore witness to him. As for him (ﷺ), he bore witness to no one, because no messenger came after him.

The scholars said regarding the word *"comprehensively"* (Saba': 28) that it means to all people together. In another place He, exalted, says: *"Say: O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of God to you all"* (Al-A'raf: 158).

That is, there is no longer any particularity, neither temporal nor spatial. When we reflect on the word *"comprehensively,"* we find it has a parallel in the reality of our language, which has settled on the tongues of the common people. We see, for example, the tailor who, when sewing a garment, uses the scissors on the cloth and cuts it into weft and warp, but the threads of the garment come out through its edges, as we say the cloth "unravels" (*binsil*). So the tailor gathers these edges together, so that the edges of the cloth are turned inward. We call this operation *kafkafat* (folding in) the cloth, or we now call it *as-sarfala* (hemming).

From this comes the word *kāffah*, meaning: gathering the scattered people in every time and place, so that no kind or group is excluded, and no one deviates from his method.

Among us farmers there is a plant that grows on the edges of canals called *najīl* (a creeping grass). It is not the well-known grass, and *najīl* does not rise above the surface of the earth, and its stalks and roots intertwine so that they prevent these edges from collapsing, or the debris from falling and blocking the canal. So it is as if the *najīl* performs a task: holding back the debris and preventing it from collapsing. That is, it restrains a kind from straying from its mission.

The word *kāffah* comes from *kaffa al-shay'* (he restrains the thing), so he is *kāff*, and the feminine *tā'* was added for emphasis, as in *'ālim*, *'allām*, and *'allāmah*. Therefore our Lord says of Himself, glorified be He: *"Knower of the unseen"* (At-Tawbah: 78). If you say: why did He not say *'allāmah*? We say: because God's knowledge does not ascend in eloquence and scarcity.

So the meaning of *"And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind"* (Saba': 28) is: you restrain them and prevent them from every evil that corrupts righteousness on earth. This is the mission of the method that our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), brought. Therefore He, glorified be He, said: *"And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation"* (Al-A'raf: 56).

So, the word *"comprehensively"* (Saba': 28) is either a description of mankind, meaning all of them, or a description of the Messenger of God, meaning one who restrains mankind from evil, and the *tā'* is for emphasis.

The meaning of *"bearer of good tidings and warner"* (Saba': 28): *bishāra* (good tidings) means informing someone of good that has not yet come at its time, and its counterpart is *nidhāra* (warning), which means informing someone of evil that has not yet come at its time. The characteristic of good tidings is that we inform you of the good coming to you, so that you take up its causes, turn toward it, and strive for it, while you yearn for it. Likewise, warning alerts you to the approaching danger, so that you turn away from its causes and repel it from yourself.

An example of this is the teacher who gives good tidings to the diligent student of success and excellence, and warns the negligent one of failure and falling behind. Why? Because he wants the diligent one to increase his diligence, and the lazy, negligent one to abandon laziness and negligence so that he too may excel.

As for His saying: *"But most of mankind do not know"* (Saba': 28): that is, they do not know that you are the Seal of the Messengers, or the messenger who came to prevent evil from all humanity and to reform its course. Since most people do not know, it means that the few are the ones who know, and this knowing minority is the leaven of good in existence. Therefore we see that however much people exaggerate in atheism and in departing from the path of truth, there must emerge from among them this few who hold fast to the truth, seek it, and call to it. They exist in every time and place, however few they may be.

Therefore our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), says: [hadith text not included in passage]. So this few must remain among us as models and cells of good, and as a means of preserving good among people, however much the world darkens around them.

Then the Truth, glorified be He, says:

﴿And they say: "When is this promise...?"﴾

The careful reader of the Book of Allah finds that the Truth, glory be to Him, did not make the Qur'an into separate chapters, one for prayer, another for zakat, another for usury... etc. Rather, He mixes these rulings in a wondrous arrangement and a fascinating blend, alternating between styles, so that its reader never tires of it and never loses interest.

The Qur'an is not a book of law that devotes a section to every crime. Rather, it deals with the crime in a unique manner: it mentions the crime, makes it appear abominable, and explains its effect. Then, when it prescribes the punishment for it, you find this punishment natural, accepted by souls, because the one who receives the punishment deserves it.

Allah, exalted is He, says, relating about the disbelievers: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Saba': 29]. A promise is only of good, and a threat is of evil. It is strange that the disbelievers should call the Resurrection a "promise." It would have been fitting for them to say, "When is this threat?" Or: Allah, exalted is He, twisted their tongues so that they uttered a word of truth, for it is indeed a promise of truth from Allah, although it is a threat for them.

The promise of Allah contains many things. Its conclusion is the Resurrection and the Reckoning, then Paradise or the Fire. But is the promise of Allah fulfilled only in the Hereafter? They said: No, rather they see some of it in this world. Otherwise, if Allah left them safe until He punished them in the Hereafter, their corruption would have spread, and those who do not believe would have acted wantonly with no one to restrain them.

Therefore, it is among His wisdom, exalted is He, that He hastens for them some of His promise, so that they see it in this world, as He says: ﴿They will be routed, and they will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45]. Indeed, the Day of Badr came, and Allah defeated them; some of them were killed, and some of them were taken captive. Just as the premises were fulfilled concerning them, so the consequences will be fulfilled in the Hereafter.

Therefore the Truth addresses His Prophet (ﷺ) saying: ﴿So whether We show you some of what We promise them, or We cause you to die, to Us they will be returned﴾ [Ghafir: 77].

So whoever does not see the promise of Allah fulfilled in this world, which you witness with your own eyes, then his promise is the Hereafter. Otherwise, there were among the disbelievers those who died before Badr and did not witness the victories and conquests of the Muslims, and no part of the punishment of this world reached them.

Their saying, ﴿When is this promise?﴾ [Saba': 29] is a request for the punishment to be hastened.

Then Allah, exalted is He, commands His Prophet to answer them: ﴿Say, "For you is an appointment of a Day from which you cannot remain behind an hour, nor can you precede it."﴾ [Saba': 30] It is the day of victory over them, as in the Day of Badr, when Allah made them taste humiliation, abasement and death, and brought an end to their arrogance. Or it is the Day of Resurrection.

He who set this appointment for you is the One Able to carry it out, and there is no power that can prevent Him, glory be to Him, from fulfilling what He promised, or even delaying it for a single moment. He, glory be to Him, knows that the cosmic signs do not deviate from what He wills.

We have previously explained that human beings, when they make promises, do not possess the means to fulfil their promises. Therefore our Lord, Mighty and Majestic is He, taught us to take precaution in this matter; He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow, * Unless Allah wills."﴾ [al-Kahf: 23-24].

Because Allah loves for His servant to be truthful, when he makes his action contingent upon the will of Allah, he spares himself from lying and from breaking his promise when he is unable to fulfil it, especially since he does not possess a single one of its elements. So, in sum: refer the matter to the One who possesses all these elements. Therefore we call a promise from people a "promise," but from Allah it is "the true promise," meaning: the one that never fails at all.

The meaning of ﴿you cannot remain behind it an hour, nor can you precede it﴾ [Saba': 30] is that it is a precisely fixed appointment. The Truth, glory be to Him, intends by this that man should keep in mind all the provisions that Allah has granted him, and that they should always remain in his mind, never neglected.

The word "day" (yawm) came indefinite and vague, and the vagueness here is itself the clarification, as we have previously made clear. When Allah, for example, leaves the term of a person's life vague, he remains constantly mindful of it, awaiting it at any time, expecting it with every breath and every moment, without tying it to an illness or anything else, for death without apparent causes is itself the cause.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "We will never believe in this Qur'an or in that which is before it..."﴾.

Then Allah commands His Prophet to respond to them: "Say: For you is the appointment of a Day from which you cannot delay by an hour, nor advance."

It is the day of victory over them, as on the Day of Badr, when Allah made them taste humiliation, abasement and death, and brought their arrogance to an end. Or it is the Day of Resurrection.

The One who set this appointment for you is capable of carrying it out, and no power can prevent Him, glorified is He, from fulfilling what He has promised, or even from delaying it for a single moment. He, glorified is He, knows that the cosmic signs do not deviate from what He wills.

We have already explained that when people make promises, they do not possess the means to fulfil them. For this reason our Lord, Mighty and Majestic is He, taught us to take precaution in this matter. He, glorified is He, said:

﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," except [with the condition], "If Allah wills."﴾ [al-Kahf: 23-24].

Because Allah loves for His servant to be truthful, when he makes his action conditional upon the will of Allah, he spares himself from lying and from breaking his promise when he fails to fulfil it. He does not possess a single element of its components. So, in sum: refer the matter to the One who possesses all these elements. For this reason we call a promise from people "wa'd" (a promise), while the promise from Allah is "al-wa'd al-haqq" (the true promise), meaning the one that never fails at all.

The meaning of "you cannot delay by an hour, nor advance" is that it is a precisely fixed appointment. The Truth, glorified is He, intended by this that a person should constantly keep in mind all the provisions that Allah has bestowed upon him, and that they should never leave his mind, so that he never becomes heedless of them.

The word "yawm" (a day) came indefinite and ambiguous, and the ambiguity here is itself the clarification, as we have previously explained. For when Allah leaves a person's term ambiguous, the person remains constantly mindful of it, awaiting it at any time, expecting it with every breath and every moment, without tying it to an illness or anything else, since death without apparent causes is itself the cause.

Their saying, "We will never believe in this Qur'an," shows their confusion (lajlaja). In another place the Qur'an relates their saying:

"Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?" [az-Zukhruf: 31] The meaning of this is that the Qur'an is free of any blemish or objection; the objection is directed at the one upon whom the Qur'an was sent down. Likewise, from their foolishness is their saying:

"If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched from our land..." [al-Qasas: 57] Thus they acknowledged that he had come with guidance.

Similar to this is their saying: "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God..." [al-Munafiqun: 7].

It is true that falsehood is confused (lajlaj); it staggers here and there in disordered thinking that has no single thread (siyal wahid), and this staggering reveals what they are upon of falsehood. We have said that the skilled investigator is the one who reaches the truth through questioning the accused in a way that trips him up without his knowing, because the one who speaks the truth relates a reality in one unchanging form: however often you repeat the question to him, he gives one answer.

As for the liar, he does not relate a reality; he relates falsehood and fabrication, which must end in contradiction in his statements...

After they said this speech, the Truthful, glorified is He, wished to make their response more terrifying, so He said: "And if you could see..." meaning: O Muhammad, "when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord," meaning: in the presence of God, awaiting judgment and reckoning.

You know that (law) (lau) is a conditional particle that requires an answer. This answer has been omitted from the context of the verse to indicate awesomeness and dread. Its estimated form is: "And if you could see, when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord... you would see a tremendous matter." In this style the soul goes in every direction, and we imagine the kinds of punishment and humiliation that the disbelievers suffer in this situation before God, the Mighty and Majestic. So omitting the answer here is more eloquent than mentioning it...

Then the verse continues describing the state of these wrongdoers before God, the Exalted. Would that it ended at humiliation and brokenness! Rather, "they cast the saying back to one another" (yarji'u ba'dhuhum ila ba'din al-qawl), meaning: they argue and debate with one another, each one throwing the blame onto the other. The word (yarji') means "mutual returning" (muraja'a): one says, and the other returns his speech and denies it. The Qur'an contains many passages relating this mutual exchange between the followers and those they followed, and here is one example:

"Those who were deemed weak will say to those who were arrogant, 'Were it not for you, we would have been believers.'" Meaning: the weak and the imitators say to the arrogant, the great leaders who were followed. It is enough of the greatness of the Resurrection that the weak one stands before the strong one, returns speech to him and confronts him, even though both are defeated and lost. That is because weakness existed in the world, along with arrogance and following; but now, in the place of reckoning, the heads are equal, and here the weak are saying to their masters, "Were it not for you, we would have been believers."

Since the matter is one of mutual returning, each returning his speech to the other, the ones who were arrogant must respond, and must return speech to those who were made weak.

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says:

"Those who were arrogant will say to those who were made weak, 'Did we turn you away...?'"

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 34, verse 32:
